In essence, this chapter presents a comprehensive guide to the different quality
management scenarios that can be implemented in SAP EWM. We’ll include the
essential configuration steps, master data, and end-to-end process demonstrations for
each scenario. By the end of this chapter, you will have a better understanding of how
SAP EWM can be integrated with quality management, thereby enabling your company
to streamline its quality management process.
3.1 Overview of Quality Management in SAP EWM
In this section, we’ll present an overview of quality management in SAP EWM,
including its architecture and deployment options. We’ll discuss the key terminology
used with quality management, then dive into the strategy for maintaining inspection
rules.
SAP EWM employs a thorough quality management system that comprises diverse
processes, procedures, and tools to guarantee the conformity of stored goods and
materials with the appropriate quality standards and to ensure that warehouse
operations meet the required standards. The main goal of quality management in SAP
EWM is to ensure uniform product quality, minimize the risk of defects and errors, and
enhance customer satisfaction. The essential elements of quality management in SAP
EWM encompass quality inspection, quality control, quality documentation, non-
conformance management, and continuous improvement.
SAP EWM’s quality management functionality guarantees products received and
packaging meet your quality criteria. The Quality Inspection Engine is utilized to
execute inspection processes in the warehouse. The Quality Inspection Engine can be
employed to conduct quality inspections exclusively in SAP EWM or can be merged
with the Quality Management (QM) component of SAP ERP if you have previously
configured it.
For more intricate quality management procedures, the Quality Inspection Engine can
be linked to an external quality management system, like QM in SAP ERP, that includes
comprehensive analytical inspections and characteristics. Once an inspection
document is initiated in SAP EWM, the Quality Inspection Engine prompts the creation
of an inspection lot in the quality management function of the enterprise resource
planning (ERP) system. The inspection procedure is then performed in the external
system, which is the ERP quality management system. Once the inspection process is
completed, the ERP quality management transmits the usage decision back to the
Quality Inspection Engine. This option is available for both SAP EWM connected to ERP
or SAP S/4HANA systems, whether they are SAP S/4HANA or non-SAP S/4HANA (ERP).

Next, we’ll discuss some key terminology. In SAP EWM, quality management
encompasses the utilization of several essential concepts to handle goods inspections
and uphold quality. Let’s consider the following terms:
Inspection object types
An inspection object type refers to the software component, process, and object for
which an inspection document can be created in the Quality Inspection Engine.
Different types of inspection object types, including Preliminary Inspection of
Inbound delivery (IOT1), Counting Inbound delivery (IOT2), Q-Inspection of Return
delivery (IOT3), Q-Inspection Product/Batch Inbound delivery (IOT4), Q-Inspection
of Product/ Batch Warehouse – Internal (IOT5), and Preliminary Inspection of
Handling Unit (IOT6).
Note
As per SAP Note 2861813, inspection object types IOT1, IO2 and IOT6 will no longer
be supported by embedded EWM systems, whereas for embedded EWM the return
processing (formally IOT3) was integrated to advanced returns management.
Inspection types
Inspection types are used to define the controls associated with each inspection.
The type of inspection determines how an inspection is carried out.
Inspection rules
Inspection rules, on the other hand, provide guidelines for creating an inspection
document. These rules are assigned to inspection object types and determine if an
© 

159
object (delivery, product, or batch) will be subject to quality inspections or not.
Some characteristics of inspection rules include an inspection procedure (e.g., 100%
inspection versus no inspection), a sample drawing procedure, dynamic
modifications, and document types.
In a decentralized system, the SAP EWM module in SAP S/4HANA is responsible for
quality management using inspection rules. These rules are maintained as master
data, and inspection documents are created in the SAP EWM system based on this
data. Additionally, an inspection lot is generated in the SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA
system. With the release of SAP S/4HANA 1909, inspection rules can now be
automatically synchronized from an ERP or SAP S/4HANA system, thus streamlining
the process even further, as shown in Figure 3.5.
In a decentralized EWM system (version 9.5 or below) and where SAP S/4HANA is not
used, quality management in SAP EWM is carried out using inspection rules. These
rules are maintained as master data, and inspection documents are created in the
SAP EWM system based on this data. Additionally, an inspection lot is generated in
the SAP ERP or SAP S/4HANA system, as shown in Figure 3.6.

Inspection lots are generated for all goods movements that are pertinent to quality
management. The material master determines which goods movements are
relevant to quality management. In the quality management module, inspections
can be planned, and all materials can be prepared at this stage. Each material can
be assigned appropriate inspection types, and the inspection configuration can be
modified as required. The inspection setup in decentralized EWM is shown in
Figure 3.7.

Figure 3.8 Inspection Setup in Embedded EWM
Decision codes
Using decision codes, you can indicate whether a sample is accepted, assign a
quality score, and specify any necessary follow-up actions. These codes are
organized into code groups, which are subsequently linked to inspection rules in a
hierarchical manner (inspection rules < decision groups < decision codes).
Findings
During the processing of an inspection document, inspection outcomes can be
documented in the form of characteristic values or findings. The requirements for
findings would depend on the item being inspected and the type of inspection being
conducted.
Follow-up sections
You can initiate a series of follow-up processes, such as putaway, stock transfer,
scrapping, or return delivery, by employing logical actions. These logical actions will
generate warehouse documents and tasks.

The inspection object type serves to define the business process for inspections; the
object to be inspected (e.g., product, HU, or delivery); and the warehouse number.
Each inspection object type can have multiple inspection rules, which determine the
criteria for triggering inspections and specify inspection details such as the process,
procedure, frequency, and codes.
During the inspection process, the system creates multiple inspection documents
based on the inspection rules. These documents contain the inspection specifications
and are used to collect inspection results, findings, and usage decisions for the
inspected object. Each inspection document can have multiple items and samples
assigned to it, and there can be multiple findings associated with each document.
However, there can only be one decision. A follow-up action, such as putaway or
scrapping, can be assigned to the usage decision.

3.2 Inspection Product/Batch for Inbound
Deliveries
SAP EWM offers various inspection processes for product/batch inbound
delivery, such as the following:
Inspection after goods receipt from external procurement (with
inspection rule)
In this process, individual products or batches are subject to inspection
during the goods receipt process, controlled by inspection object type IOT4.
Pre-sampling in production or inspection after goods receipt (SAP EWM
9.2 and higher)
Pre-sampling is a process utilized for internally produced goods in SAP EWM.
Acceptance sampling (SAP EWM 9.2 and higher)
Before posting a goods receipt for externally procured goods, a necessary step
is to conduct a quality inspection. Acceptance sampling can be used to
determine whether to allow or block a goods receipt and, if allowed, whether
to impose restrictions until a usage decision is made. If a restricted goods
receipt is allowed, the stock category for the goods receipt posting (e.g.,
blocked stock) can be defined through the configuration of the follow-up
action.
Additionally, acceptance sampling can be combined with inspection control
after goods receipt. For example, based on the acceptance sample result, a
decision can be made to allow a restricted goods receipt into blocked stock,
followed by a more detailed inspection after goods receipt. To combine
acceptance sampling with inspection control after goods receipt, an
inspection rule must be maintained for both acceptance sampling and
inspections after goods receipt.
We’ll discuss the first two options in more depth in the following sections.
Because acceptance sampling is not commonly used, we won’t cover that topic
further in this chapter.

3.2.1 Inspection after Goods Receipts from External
Procurement (With Inspection Rule)
The inspection process following the receipt of goods from external
procurement with inspection rule is available in SAP EWM 5.0 and higher.
Individual products or batches are subject to inspection during the goods
receipt process, controlled by IOT4. Depending on the system configuration, the
inspection document is generated either upon activation of the inbound
delivery or when the inbound delivery status is set to In Yard.
In this section, we’ll cover the business scenario, configuration, and master data
setup needed for inspections after goods receipt from external procurement
with an inspection rule. We’ll then walk you step-by-step through a process
demo.

As shown in Figure 3.10, an inspection process is initiated in SAP EWM in one of
two ways: activating an inbound delivery or setting the In Yard status.
Figure 3.10 Inspection after Goods Receipt: External Procurement

In SAP EWM, the goods receipt for the inbound delivery is completed.
Upon completing the full goods receipt or the first partial goods receipt,
SAP EWM releases the inspection document.

inspection document. If any active inspection object types are related to a
particular process and object, the inspection document will be
automatically created using the inspection rules. To maintain inspection
©

3.3.2 Recurring Inspections (With Inspection Rules)
Some industries, such as chemicals and pharmaceuticals, require regular
inspections of batch-managed products in the warehouse. A recurring
inspection is a type of warehouse-internal inspection that is not related to
inbound or outbound processes, but rather to internal warehouse processes.
Recurring inspections are essential for batch-managed products, but they can

Business Scenario
As shown in Figure 3.72, the system can determine the date of next inspection

LOBM_QNDAT (next inspection date) to the batch.

When a new batch is created, the system automatically assigns the next

If the manufacturing date is available for the batch, the system calculates the

the material/product master) to the manufacturing date.
If the manufacturing date is NOT available for the batch, the system calculates
the next inspection date by adding the inspection interval (which is
maintained in the material/product master) to the batch creation date.

This remarkable quality management component of SAP EWM means you can
conduct meticulous inspections on returned items, thereby significantly
enhancing the efficiency and transparency of the entire process. To initiate the
returns process, you can create either an advanced returns management returns
order or a returns stock transport order. Consequently, you’re presented with
two distinct options for conducting comprehensive quality inspections:
Option 1: Performing the inspection prior to the goods being received in
the SAP ERP system via advanced returns management
Option 1 entails carrying out the inspection, making a decision, and
performing subsequent logistical actions entirely within the SAP ERP system.
